topic: Rome had a pee tax (Vespasian's urine tax)
pillar: Past: wild true story (brain-rot format test)

claims.claim: Roman fullers (launderers) used urine, rich in ammonia, to clean and bleach wool clothing such as togas.
Emperor Vespasian (AD 69-79) taxed urine collected from Rome's public toilets; the buyers (fullers, tanners) paid it.
claims.note: Script says he taxed the public toilets' pee - not 'everyone's pee'.

claims.claim: Suetonius (Vespasian 23): his son Titus objected; Vespasian held a coin from the first payment to Titus's nose and asked if it smelled; Titus said no; Vespasian replied that it came from urine.
claims.note: Told as reported speech, no invented quotes.

claims.claim: The saying 'pecunia non olet' - 'money doesn't stink' - comes from this story.
Public urinals in France were called 'vespasiennes' (and 'vespasiani' in Italy) after him.
